title: Extreme First-Passage Time of Many Interacting Particles
abstract: Extreme first-passage events are broadly relevant to biological, chemical, and physical processes in which the first successful arrival determines the outcome. Existing theories are confined to noninteracting searchers. Interacting extreme-statistics problems are notoriously difficult because correlations destroy probability factorization. We establish a general framework for interacting extreme search. A no-go theorem shows that broad classes of bounded interactions cannot beat the $1/\ln N$ extreme timescale of $N$ independent Brownian searchers, and complementary upper bounds prove that this scale is exact for broad classes of repulsive interactions. We then identify two sharp mechanisms beyond the logarithmic class and derive a unified interaction-driven acceleration limit. In particular, deterministic pairwise interaction can at most reduce the extreme search time to order $1/N$, while stochastic pairwise forcing attains $1/(N\ln N)$. Our results separate acceleration due to statistical redundancy from that generated by coherent many-body transport or amplified fluctuations, deepening our understanding of interacting stochastic systems.
summary: This paper develops a general theoretical framework to calculate the extreme first-passage time for multiple diffusing particles that interact with each other. It proves that while statistical effects limit this time to $1/\ln N$, specific coherent interactions can accelerate the process, achieving rates as fast as $1/N$ or $1/(N \ln N)$. The work deepens understanding by separating acceleration sources into those from redundancy versus those from collective transport.
main_problem: The research addresses determining the extreme first-passage time (EFPT) for multiple interacting particles to reach a target, especially when this earliest arrival dictates the outcome of a physical process.
main_result: The authors establish that while independent searchers yield an EFPT scaling of $1/\ln N$, interactions can accelerate this rate up to deterministic pairwise interaction ($O(1/N)$) or stochastic forcing ($O(1/(N \ln N))$).
method: The work employs rigorous probabilistic bounding techniques, including establishing no-go theorems and deriving unified lower bounds by analyzing the interplay between coherent drift and enhanced diffusion.
model_or_system: The model consists of $N$ overdamped searchers diffusing in a $d$-dimensional space towards an absorbing target set $\Gamma$, governed by Langevin dynamics with various interaction potentials (e.g., repulsive, deterministic).
key_observables: Extreme first-passage time ($T_N$), initial minimum distance ($\ell_0$), and the scaling exponents related to drift ($B_N$) and effective diffusion ($	ext{Deff}_N$).
important_parameters: The number of particles $N$, the dimensionality $d$, and the nature/strength of the pairwise interactions.
main_assumptions: Key results rely on assumptions about bounded interactions, specific initial-state control (e.g., local coordination $\mathrm{M}_N$), or analyzing short-time logarithmic windows.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scaling differences between independent searchers and those subjected to various interaction mechanisms, showing how different resource types (drift vs. diffusion) determine the lower bound on $T_N$.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the benchmark for non-interacting particles ($1/\ln N$) via a no-go theorem, then systematically deriving sharp upper and lower bounds by identifying specific mechanisms—deterministic drift or stochastic forcing—that lead to faster acceleration regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical diffusion, the rigorous mathematical framework for bounding collective transport times in interacting systems is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems, such as reaction rates or quench dynamics where rare events dominate.
